title: Course Overview
summary: CSS360 surveys software engineering processes, tools, and techniques used in development and quality assurance.
details: The course covers life-cycle models, requirements analysis, quality assurance, verification, validation, testing, and project planning.
Prerequisites include completion of a two-course programming sequence.
CSS360 serves as a prerequisite for CSS 370.

title: Class Meeting Schedule
summary: Class meets twice weekly on Tuesday and Thursday from 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM.
details: Sessions are scheduled for a maximum of 120 minutes with a break halfway through.
The instructor aims to end sessions a bit early when possible.
Meetings happen at the normal time and place unless the instructor communicates otherwise.

title: Class Meeting Location
summary: In-person meetings are held in UW1 building room 302.
details: Plan to attend in person at the scheduled location unless an announcement indicates a change.
During extreme weather, the instructor may hold class via Zoom instead of in person and will communicate through announcements.

title: Instructor
summary: The course instructor is Kaylea Champion.
details: Students may address the instructor as Doctor Champion or Professor Champion.
There is another instructor named Champion in the department; this course is taught by Kaylea Champion.

title: Required Textbook
summary: There is no required textbook for this course.
details: Course materials come from a wide range of sources that should be free when accessed through Canvas or the UW Library Proxy.
If you have difficulty accessing any material, notify the instructor promptly via a public Discord message.

title: Flipped Classroom Format
summary: The course uses a flipped format where students prepare asynchronously and use class time for discussion and project work.
details: Readings, recorded lectures, tutorials, and assignments are completed outside of class meeting times.
The instructor does not generally deliver lectures during synchronous class meetings.
Class time is used for standups, case discussions, questions, and assignment support.

title: Expected Weekly Workload
summary: As a 5-credit course, plan for roughly 10 hours of weekly coursework plus 4 hours in class and up to 1 hour in lab or office hours.
details: If you are spending substantially more time than expected, consider booking an office hours appointment to discuss learning strategies.
Spending substantially less time may mean missing opportunities to learn, grow, and demonstrate skills.

title: Preferred Contact Order
summary: Contact the instructor in this order: public Discord, private Discord, Canvas for grades, and email only when necessary.
details: Public Discord messages help others who may have the same question or answer.
Private Discord works for individual questions that do not need to be public.
All grade-related discussion must happen via Canvas, not Discord or email.

title: Asking Questions on Discord
summary: Discord is the preferred channel for most course questions and asynchronous discussion.
details: Discord supports text, voice, and screensharing for course communication between class sessions.
Questions posted publicly allow classmates to see answers and learn from them.
If you are unsure which channel to use, ask in the general discussion channel.

title: Grade Discussions on Canvas
summary: All grade-related discussion must take place through Canvas, not Discord or email.
details: Use Canvas for conversations about grades, comments, and assessment feedback.
For grade questions, book a private calendar timeslot within one week of the grade being released.

title: Email as a Last Resort
summary: Use email only when absolutely necessary for course communication.
details: Discord is preferred for most questions because answers can benefit the whole class.
Polite and focused messages receive faster replies; unprofessional messages may be filtered.

title: Response Time and Follow-Up
summary: If the instructor has not responded within 48 hours, send a polite follow-up via Discord direct message.
details: A non-response within 48 hours is unintentional and often due to high message volume.
The instructor checks and responds to Discord conversation at least daily throughout the quarter.

title: Reporting an Absence
summary: Submit the course absence form at least one hour before class if you will miss, arrive late, or leave early.
details: The absence form alerts the instructor so you are not treated as a no-call, no-show.
Filing the form avoids a penalty tied to unreported absences but does not create a makeup opportunity.
The form is hosted as a Google Docs web form linked from the course page.

title: Impact of Missing Class
summary: Missing class affects in-class participation grades and cold-call opportunities.
details: Not filing the absence form counts as a no-call, no-show and impacts the in-class activities grade.
After an absence, you may be called upon more often in later classes to balance participation.
Missing too many classes can make it impossible to earn full credit for in-class activities.

title: No Makeup for In-Class Activities
summary: There is no direct way to make up missed in-class activities such as case discussion participation.
details: Advance notice through the absence form avoids a no-call, no-show penalty but is not a makeup.
You are responsible for obtaining notes, handouts, and assignment information you miss.
Lab completion counts as answering two in-class questions and may be completed outside of class.

title: Standup Attendance
summary: Standup participation requires being present and actively participating during the synchronous standup meeting.
details: Standup participation is equivalent to answering one in-class question for grading purposes.
There is no direct makeup for missing a standup; sharing an update on Discord is helpful but not a substitute.
You must document standup work on Discord to receive standup credit.

title: Before-Class Preparation
summary: Complete all assigned readings and recorded lectures before the associated class session.
details: You are fully responsible for finishing readings and lecture material before coming to class.
The instructor expects regular check-in and participation in the course Discord server throughout the week.
Come to class prepared for cold-call discussion and team activities.

title: Reading Notes and Cold Calling
summary: Case discussions use cold calling, but Reading Note questions are finalized at least six days in advance for preparation.
details: The instructor will not summarize case material in class; students are expected to have read it.
Cold calls use only questions from distributed Reading Notes or formats announced far enough ahead to prepare.
Writing out answers in advance is recommended, though Reading Notes are not collected.

title: Assignment Due Times
summary: Unless otherwise noted, assignments are due at the end of the day at 11:59 PM Pacific time.
details: End of day means 11:59 PM on the listed due date in the Pacific time zone.
Some due dates in the schedule are listed as Seattle time, which follows Pacific time for this course.

title: Course Assignments Overview
summary: The course includes one group project, one reflection essay, and short low-stakes quizzes.
details: Assignments give hands-on practice with software engineering concepts taught in class.
The reflection essay draws on course concepts and evidence from the bot project experience.
Students are responsible for verifying that the correct file is submitted on Canvas.

title: Quizzes and Exams
summary: There are no exams in this course, but there may be short, low-stakes quizzes.
details: Quizzes, when used, are intentionally short and low-stakes rather than high-pressure assessments.
There is no final exam; the March 17 timeslot is a designated co-working period with optional open lab instead of a meeting.

title: File Submission Responsibility
summary: Students must verify that the correct file is submitted on Canvas for each assignment.
details: Canvas is used for announcements, restricted files, assignment submission, and grade distribution.
Contact UW-IT or consult Canvas support resources if you have technical difficulties with submission.

title: Discord Bot Group Project
summary: Students work in groups to build, analyze, and deploy a Discord bot across multiple sprint tasks.
sourceSection: Project: Developing a Discord Bot as a Team
details: The default project is a Discord bot, though teams may propose alternative bot ideas early in the quarter.
Project tasks build on one another from environment setup through version 2.1 release.
Group process and behavioral traces in course tools are part of how project work is assessed.

title: Sprint Planning and Standups
summary: Teams conduct sprint planning to commit to user stories and hold standups at the start of each class.
details: In sprint planning, teams review the sprint backlog and commit to user stories for the sprint.
Standups cover what you did since the last standup, what you will do next, and any blockers.
GitHub work done during sprint planning is scored as part of the sprint grade.

title: GitHub Workflow Expectations
summary: Project work uses GitHub repositories, Kanban boards, feature branches, pull requests, and release tags.
details: Each group maintains a GitHub project environment with a Kanban board to track work.
Use feature branches and pull requests to merge work into the team main branch.
Tag releases clearly (for example, version 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1) with release notes and updated documentation.

title: Bot Demonstrations
summary: Version 2.0 of the bot is demonstrated through both a pre-recorded demo and a live in-class presentation.
details: Each group member records an individual pre-made screencast demo of the bot in action.
Live demos occur in class with the full group participating in a timed presentation slot.
Demo grades reflect preparation and participation; have pre-recorded demos ready as a fallback.

title: Reflection Essay Requirements
summary: The reflection is a 1000–1500 word essay connecting course concepts to your bot project experience.
sourceSection: Reflection on Software Engineering and the Bot Project
details: Use real evidence from your project, such as commit IDs, line numbers, and dates.
Cite sources that are real and viewable; fabricated citations are academic misconduct.
AI tools are forbidden for the reflection assignment.

title: Grade Weights
summary: Grades combine in-class activities, three sprints, presentation work, and the reflection.
details: In-class activities, including labs and case discussion: 50%.
Sprint 1: 10%, Sprint 2: 15%, Sprint 3: 15%.
Presentation (demo, pre-made demo, and feedback): 5%. Reflection: 5%.

title: Percentage to 4.0 Scale
summary: Overall course percentage maps to the UW 4.0 scale with 97.0% equal to 4.0 and 60.0% equal to 0.7.
details: Grades are spaced evenly between 97.0% (4.0) and 60.0% (0.7) for this quarter.
A 2.0 requires at least 74.6% in the course.
Doing the bare minimum is a high-risk approach because later disruptions can affect your grade.

title: Late Work Policy
summary: Among Bot Project Tasks 1–6, you may use one no-questions-asked 48-hour extension per quarter.
details: Request the extension privately through Canvas so it is trackable.
Late work receives a 20% penalty for each 48-hour period after the deadline.
No extension is available for demo, feedback, or reflection assignments due to tight coordination and end-of-quarter timing.

title: AI Tools Policy
summary: AI use is permitted only when assignment instructions allow it, and all AI sources must be cited.
details: Students are responsible for verifying that AI-generated information is accurate.
Be careful about privacy: many AI tools may incorporate content you share.
Some assignments explicitly prohibit AI, including the reflection and bot feedback assignments.
Grammar and spellchecking with AI is allowed even when other AI uses are restricted.

title: Office Hours and Open Lab
summary: Book office hours at least 24 hours in advance; open lab periods are optional drop-in times separate from appointments.
details: Office hour appointments guarantee focused one-on-one attention.
If you book less than 24 hours in advance, confirm the booking with a Discord message.
Open lab offers time to ask questions and work on assignments with help available, but attendance is optional.

title: Required Technology
summary: The course expects reliable access to Canvas, Discord, GitHub, Google Docs, Panopto, and the UW Library Proxy.
details: Canvas handles announcements, files, submissions, and grades.
GitHub is required for project work; Google Docs hosts forms such as the absence form.
Panopto hosts recorded lectures. Off-campus access to restricted materials may require the UW Library Proxy or VPN.

title: Dynamic Syllabus Updates
summary: The syllabus is a dynamic document; monitor Canvas announcements and the syllabus wiki for changes.
details: Core expectations are fixed, but project details, readings, and assignments may shift during the quarter.
Readings generally will not change within six days of their due date.
The instructor summarizes syllabus changes in weekly Canvas announcements; wiki history tracks edits.
